title: Review: Atoms and nuclear radiation; Hazards and uses of radioactive emissions and of background radiation (physics only)
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank for AQA GCSE Physics (8463) (review status in the bank: authored-gated-unreviewed). Terms: 4.4.3-c09, 4.4.3-c03, 4.4.2-c15, 4.4.2-c23. Clues: 4.4.3-c09 written for the game from the bank's definition; 4.4.3-c03 first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.4.2-c15 first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.4.2-c23 written for the game from the bank's definition. Questions: 4.4.3-q06, 4.4.3-q07, 4.4.3-q08, 4.4.3-q09, 4.4.2-q23, 4.4.2-q32, 4.4.3-q05, 4.4.3-q12, 4.4.3-q17, 4.4.2-q25, 4.4.2-q29, 4.4.3-q02. The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Sievert (Sv)
items.clue: The unit of exposure risk, often quoted in thousandths.

items.label: Cosmic rays
items.clue: Ionising radiation that arrives at the Earth from space.

items.label: Ionising power
items.clue: How strongly radiation removes electrons from the atoms it passes.

items.label: Half-life
items.clue: The time taken for the count rate from a sample of an isotope to fall to 50% of its starting value.

questions.stem: People living where the local rock is granite, and aircrew who fly long-haul routes, both receive above-average annual radiation doses. Which statement explains both cases?

options.text: Fallout from nuclear weapons tests gathers on high ground and on granite.
The aircrew's height should lower their dose, so only the granite case is real.
Location affects dose: granite gives radon, altitude gives cosmic rays.
Everyone really gets the same dose, so both averages must be wrong.

questions.stem: A safety leaflet states that a worker received a radiation dose of 4.5 mSv during one year. What does this dose value describe?

options.text: The number of counts that her detector recorded each second.
The number of nuclei that decayed in the sources she used.
The mass of radioactive material she took into her body.
The risk of harm to her body from the radiation absorbed.

questions.explanation: Radiation dose measures the risk of harm to body tissue from the radiation absorbed; it depends on the amount and the type of radiation.

questions.stem: A patient's total radiation dose over a course of treatment is 2500 mSv. Using 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv), what is this dose in sieverts?

options.text: 2.5 Sv

questions.explanation: A millisievert is one thousandth of a sievert, so 2500 mSv is divided by 1000, giving 2.5 Sv.

questions.stem: A worker's badge records a dose of 45 mSv over one year. Using 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv), what is this dose in sieverts?

options.text: 45 Sv
4.5 Sv

questions.explanation: 45 mSv divided by 1000 gives 0.045 Sv, correctly a smaller number than the value in millisieverts.

questions.stem: Which statement shows that radioactive decay is a random process?

options.text: Each nucleus in the sample decays exactly one half-life after the last.
The decay of the sample speeds up as the number of nuclei drops.
Decay can be started or stopped by heating up the sample.
It is impossible to say which nucleus will decay next, or when.

questions.explanation: Unpredictability of the individual event is exactly what randomness means here.

questions.stem: Studies of the effects of radiation on humans are published and shared with other scientists. Why does this matter?

options.text: So that members of the public can vote on whether the work is right.
So that the government decides which findings should be believed.
So that other scientists check the findings by peer review.
So that the researchers are paid for all of the work they did.

questions.explanation: The specification requires findings to be shared so they can be checked by peer review.

questions.stem: A radiographer in a hospital records a higher annual radiation dose than an office worker who lives in the same street. What is the best explanation?

options.text: Everyone receives the same dose, so the readings must be faulty.
Her occupation exposes her to radiation that the office worker never meets.
Radiation collects in the body of anybody who works indoors all day.
Both really get equal doses, so the extra reading must come from the building.

questions.explanation: The specification states that radiation dose may be affected by occupation; work with X-ray equipment and radioactive sources adds to her dose.

questions.stem: A source with a half-life of a few minutes is spilled in a school laboratory. Why is it a serious hazard at once but much less of one an hour later?

options.text: The nuclei all stop decaying once one half-life has gone by.
Its activity is high at first and then falls away fast.
A short half-life means it gives out no radiation at all.
Its radiation changes from gamma into harmless alpha rays.

questions.explanation: A short half-life means very many decays each second at the start, and that rate halves every few minutes, so the hazard is immediate but brief.

questions.stem: A gamma beam rotated around a patient destroys a deep tumour, but it also passes through healthy tissue. Evaluate this treatment.

options.text: Justified: the tumour is destroyed and the dose to healthy tissue is limited.
Ideal: careful aiming means that only the tumour receives any radiation.
Unjustified: no dose of nuclear radiation to a patient is acceptable.
Ineffective: gamma is too weakly ionising to damage a deep tumour.

questions.explanation: Rotating the beam spreads the dose to healthy tissue over a large volume while the tumour stays in the path, so the benefit outweighs the side effects.

questions.stem: If the decay of each nucleus is random, why does a sample have a definite half-life?

options.text: Because each nucleus waits its turn, so the decays are evenly spread out.
Because every nucleus is timed to decay after the same fixed period.
Because a sample holds so many nuclei that their average behaviour is predictable.
Because each half-life removes half, so two half-lives use up the whole sample.

questions.explanation: Large numbers make the statistics reliable even though each single event is unpredictable.

questions.stem: Fruit is exposed to gamma radiation from a source in order to kill bacteria on it. What happens to the fruit?

options.text: The fruit becomes radioactive and must be stored before it is sold.
The fruit becomes contaminated with atoms from the gamma source.
The fruit is irradiated, so no precautions are needed by workers.
The fruit has been irradiated; it does not become radioactive itself.

questions.explanation: Irradiation is exposure to radiation, and the irradiated object does not become radioactive.

questions.stem: Which of these is a natural source of background radiation?

options.text: Fallout still present from earlier nuclear weapons tests
Cosmic rays that reach the Earth's surface from space
Radioactive waste kept in a store at a power plant
Radiation produced by an X-ray machine in a hospital

questions.explanation: Cosmic rays from space are named in the specification as a natural source of background radiation, alongside rocks.
